input.text: Two features of the design should be borne in mind when the results are used. Trehalose is a derived rather than a measured quantity, so its apparent response is bound to that of total carbohydrate, glucose and glycogen. The untreated control was a single batch common to all analogue and timing combinations within a season, which constrains the precision of comparisons against that baseline; comparisons against the solvent control, which was applied afresh at each timing, are the more secure.

input.text: The experiment was conducted at the College of Temperate Sericulture, Mirgund, Sher-e- Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir, with the biochemical estimations carried out in the Division of Basic Sciences and Humanities, Faculty of Horticulture, Shalimar, during the spring and autumn seasons of 2021 and 2022. context.next: Three juvenile hormone analogues were compared: methoprene (isopropyl (2E,4E)-11- methoxy-3,7,11-trimethyl-2,4-dodecadienoate), fenoxycarb (ethyl N-[2-(4- phenoxyphenoxy)ethyl]carbamate) and bakuchiol, a meroterpene phenol obtained from Cullen corylifolium (L.) Medik. (syn. Psoralea corylifolia L.) Each was dissolved in ethanol and applied topically with an atomiser to larvae that had completed the fourth moult, at 0.01 (C2), 0.1 (C3) and 1.0 (C4) microlitre per 10 microlitre of ethanol per larva. An untreated batch (C0) and an ethanol-only batch (C1) served as controls. Every analogue-by-concentration combination was applied at 24 (A1), 48 (A2), 72 (A3) and 96 h (A4) after the fourth moult, giving 60 treatment combinations in each season. Larvae were hand-picked into clean trays and all residual leaf and litter removed before the analogue was applied. The trial was laid out in a completely randomised design with a factorial arrangement of the three factors; each value reported is the mean of three replications of 100 uniform larvae. The untreated control was common to the three analogues within a season.

input.text: The lakes of Bangalore are chiefly man-made. The earliest systematic accounts of the region, beginning with the survey of Mysore commissioned at the start of the nineteenth century, describe a countryside in which chains of small irrigation reservoirs, each impounded behind an earthen bund across a shallow valley, sustained rice agriculture almost entirely (Nagendra 2016). The tradition is far older: Kempe Gowda, the sixteenth-century founder of Bangalore, accompanied the fortification of his settlement with tank building, and Hebbal Lake, one of the largest of the northern lakes, is traceable to 1537 and his initiative (Ravi Kumar and Spoorthi 2025). The motive was practical – the plateau stands at about 900 m, receives a modest and erratic monsoon, and has no major perennial river, so storage was the only insurance against drought – and over the centuries rulers, landholders and village communities added tanks until the plateau held many hundreds of them.

context.heading: INTRODUCTION
context.prev: 1.7 The Tank System of Bangalore: Historical Evolution
context.next: The kere, as these tanks are known in Kannada, was never merely an engineering work: it was a village commons carrying a bundle of uses – irrigation, cattle watering, fishing, washing, silt collection and dry-season grazing of the tank bed – whose upkeep was a collective obligation rather than the duty of a distant authority (Nagendra 2016). The tanks were also linked into larger hydrological wholes: each sat on a natural drainage line and passed its surplus to the next below, forming cascades that fed the three principal valleys of the plateau – the Vrishabhavathi to the west, the Hebbal valley to the north and the Koramangala–Challaghatta system to the east and south (Gowda and Sridhara 2007) – so that a mosaic of small structures behaved in aggregate like a single regulated drainage system, with the corollary that a breach at one point had consequences all the way downstream (Figure 1).

input.text: The chemistry and biology of its water express the state of a lake, but qualitative appreciation is no substitute for measurement against agreed standards. The premise of limnological assessment is that physical, chemical and biological parameters, read together, give an integrated picture that no single variable can supply: temperature and light govern the rates of photosynthesis and decomposition; dissolved oxygen with BOD and COD registers the input and oxidation of organic matter; the major ions carry the signature of catchment and sewage; and coliform bacteria measure the sanitary risk to those who use the water. For comparability between laboratories and over time, the study followed the twenty-third edition of the Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater (APHA 2017).

context.heading: INTRODUCTION

context.next: The data are interpreted against three benchmarks. The Indian drinking-water specification IS 10500 fixes acceptable and permissible limits for the major parameters and requires the absence of Escherichia coli in 100 mL (BIS 2012); the WHO guidelines likewise require zero E. coli and set a health-based nitrate limit of 50 mg/L (WHO 2022). The designated-best-use classification assigns surface waters to classes A–E: Class A (drinking-water source after disinfection alone) demands DO ≥ 6 mg/L, BOD ≤ 2 mg/L and total coliforms ≤ 50 MPN/100 mL; Class B (outdoor bathing) DO ≥ 5, BOD ≤ 3 and coliforms ≤ 500; Class C (drinking-water source after conventional treatment) coliforms ≤ 5,000 with DO ≥ 4; Class D (wildlife and fisheries) DO ≥ 4; and Class E (irrigation and industrial cooling) conductivity ≤ 2,250 µS/cm (CPCB 2008). Few sewage-fed lakes of Bangalore meet even the Class C criteria (Ramachandra et al. 2016). The parameters examined, and the methods by which they were determined, are summarised in Figure 2.

input.text: Tracking the succession requires quantitative proxies for algal biomass and production. Chlorophyll was estimated spectrophotometrically in 80 per cent acetone extracts using the equations of Arnon (1949): chlorophyll a = 12.7 A₆₆₃ − 2.69 A₆₄₅, chlorophyll b = 22.9 A₆₄₅ − 4.68 A₆₆₃, total chlorophyll = 20.2 A₆₄₅ + 8.02 A₆₆₃, expressed per litre of filtered water. Primary productivity was measured by the classical light-and-dark bottle oxygen method: net primary production is the oxygen gain of the light bottle over the initial bottle (NPP = LB − IB), community respiration the loss in the dark bottle (R = IB − DB), and gross primary production their sum (GPP = LB − DB). Together, nutrient dosing, chlorophyll and oxygen-based productivity characterise the thresholds and the succession in units that connect directly to the field monitoring of the three study lakes.

input.text: The study covers one complete hydrological year, July 2022 to June 2023, resolved into five seasons, and three lakes of Bangalore North representing a gradient from a large eutrophic water body through a shrunken, highly polluted tank to a shallow, comparatively cleaner one; within each lake, the three-station design separates the open water, the stagnant deposit zone and the wastewater inlet, so that internal heterogeneity can be distinguished from differences among lakes. The physical, chemical and microbial analyses follow standard methods, and the floristic surveys identify algae, hydrophytes and mesophytes to the level of the genus, sufficient for the diversity and pollution-indicator analyses employed. The eutrophication experiments were conducted in vitro, their purpose being to define threshold nutrient concentrations rather than to reproduce the full complexity of the lake, so extrapolation to the field is made with caution; likewise, the zebrafish and duckweed assays serve as screening-level assessments of biological effect, not regulatory determinations of safe concentration. The study does not attempt sediment or fish-tissue residue chemistry, hydrological modelling or socio-economic survey. Within these limits, it offers a seasonally resolved, comparative and biologically anchored account of three urban wetlands, intended to inform lake management in the city and to serve as a baseline for longer-term surveillance.

input.text: Emotion detection in social media text must deal with five challenges, which include strong class imbalance, contextual ambiguity in short informal texts, hyperparameter sensitivity in deep architectures, platform-specific noise in text, and co-occurrence of multiple emotions. This paper presents a bidirectional long-term short-term memory (BiLSTM) network-augmented attention pooling with a novel end-to-end framework called HEFCSO-BiLSTM in which an attention-based optimization hybrid model, HEFCSO, consisting of the global FA and the local CSA exploration-exploitation framework, adapts the BiLSTM weights, biases, dropout rates, and the learning rate to minimize categorical cross-entropy loss. Combining domain-specific preprocessing, 200-dimensional GloVe tweet embeddings, and SMOTE-Text class balancing for end-to-end text processing, the model is extensively analyzed for this study in which three curated datasets crescent up to old benchmark corpora of SemEval-2018, ISEAR, and GoEmotions. In the combined data set, the results achieved 96.42% accuracy, 95.00% F1-score, and an MCC of 0.945 for SemEval 2018, with 10 percentage points better than the best baseline in accuracy. We conducted ablation studies, statistical significance (p < 0.05), and an analysis of the interpretability of the weights of the attention.

Multivariable logistic regression (Hosmer–Lemeshow calibration, ROC AUC discrimination, VIF multicollinearity checks, Box–Tidwell linearity test, Firth penalized sensitivity analysis) and bootstrapped mediation analysis (5,000 resamples; bias-corrected 95% CI as primary inferential result) were used.

context.prev: Objective: To describe formal employer health-insurance provision rates across Omani private-sector firms, to identify firm structural factors independently associated with provision, and to assess whether organisational resource capacity mediates the firm size–provision relationship.
context.next: Results: Formal provision was 36.5% overall (95% CI: 30.2–43.1%), ranging from 10.8% among micro-enterprises to 81.0% among large firms (Cramér’s V = 0.573, p < 0.001). The most common barriers among non-insuring firms were absence of a legal mandate (51.8%) and high premium costs (49.6%).

input.text: The covariates were chosen in advance for two reasons: (a) each measured variable has a theoretical relevance, as it has been identified in the literature as a structural or contextual determinant of employer insurance provision; and (b) the survey instrument made them available. The structure was primarily influenced by the size of the organization. The rationale for including the industry sector is that sectors differ systematically by employment contract type, informality of workforce, and visibility of regulatory oversight (Alkenbrack et al., 2015; AlJohani & Bugis, 2024). International subsidiaries inherit compliance from parent company's jurisdiction. As a result, ownership was included. As a predictor (H1) and a mediator, the capacity of the organisation’s resources was included. All pre-specified variables were included simultaneously in a forced entry model, without conducting a stepwise or data-driven selection. Check the model assumptions. In order to guarantee the linearity of logit, the Box and Tidwell procedure (Box and Tidwell, 1962) has been applied to the continuous capacity predictor. The interaction term for capacity × ln(capacity) is non-significant (p = 0.34), confirming a linear association in log-odds. All VIFs indices for predictors were below 2.0 (table 3), indicating no bias in estimates. Influential observations were evaluated for Cook’s distance values greater than 4/n = 0.018. Seven observations had larger values. Examination of the original survey records showed no implausible entries. All were included in the final model.

input.text: Pre-implementation survey of 222 Omani private-sector employers reveals three key trends. Generally speaking, formal health-insurance provision is strongly associated with firm size, ranging from 10.8% among micro-enterprises and 81.0% among large firms (Cramér’s V = 0.573). Insurance compliance is shaped by fixed costs that are found to be in line with a seven-fold gradient. Administrative costs per employee decline with scale, which gives a structural compliance advantage to bigger firms as documented by Hadley and Reschovsky 2002. The weighted estimate of 21.9% (95% CI: 17.0–26.8%) after post-stratification shows that the unweighted 36.5% reflects oversampling of micro-enterprises in the study with the weighted likely being a better estimate of coverage among national employers.

context.next: The study’s mediation analysis revealed that organizational resources statistically accounted for 30.3% of the total size-provision association (indirect effect = 0.413, bias-corrected 95% CI: 0.189–0.687). The city's built-up area increased by an estimated 584 per cent between 1973 and 2010, while vegetation cover has declined by 66 per cent and area under water bodies decreased by 74 per cent (Ramachandra et al., 2012). A subsequent study covering 105 lakes listed only 4 under good category with twenty-five rated very bad and with more than 90 per cent polluted, encroached, or both (Ramachandra et al. 2016) According to the Indian Space Research Organisation and the Karnataka Lake Conservation and Development Authority, there is independent verification. Historical satellite images show that the number of lakes within the Bangalore Development Authority area dropped by sub- divisions from 484 in 1965 to 407 in 2017. The number of lakes in the broader catchment area dropped from 1,282 to 1,191. The drainage network shrank by about 325 km in the city area.

input.text: 1.10 Limnological Assessment of Water Quality: An Overview The chemistry and biology of a lake's water express, so to speak, the state of the lake. An observer can learn a great deal from a single glance at eutrophic urban lakes, which are green, turbid, perhaps foaming at the inlet. However, this qualitative appreciation is hardly the same as taking a water sample and measurement against agreed standards. The idea behind limnological assessment is that physical,chemical and biological parameters when read together give an integrated picture of ecosystem health that is not achievable by a single variable (Wetzel 2001). The rates of photosynthesis and decomposition are governed by temperature and light; dissolved oxygen and its associated indices (BOD and COD) give an indication of organic matter input and oxidation capacity; ions (e.g. chlorides, sulphates, phosphates and nitrates) are a signature of the catchment and of sewage; and coliform bacteria reflect the health risk to people who live around and use the water.

input.text: 1.11.3 Turbidity To look at turbidity in more depth, turbidity refers to light that is scattered by suspended material. Uniform material will cause scattering but silt and clay will be washed in from the catchment. Furthermore, resuspended bottom sediments, plankton cells and organic detritus are Page 71 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 71 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 also suspended in water which causes scattering. Ambient and incident light field which are underwater tend to become attenuated because of turbidity. Wetzel (2001) notes that photosynthesis is confined to the illuminated zone, and increased turbidity decreases the euphotic depth and can constrain primary production even when nutrients are not limiting. The specifications for drinking water are stringent: 1 NTU acceptable, 5 NTU allowed only in the absence of an alternative source (BIS 2012), values which are at least one order of magnitude lower than those found in productive lakes or monsoon disturbed lakes. Turbidity shows a strong seasonal signal in tropical shallow waters. During the monsoon season, rainfall runoff brings in sas many suspended solids to shallow basins that transparency often fails, both during and posteriori to the rains. Conversely, in the still, stratified weeks of summer, suspended clay settles and water clarity may improve, until algae blooms itself become the dominant scattering agent. In this state, high turbidity indicates biological rather than mineral loading (Talling and Lemoalle 1998). The remedy for silt-laden inflow differs from that for bloom-driven turbidity and, thus, makes a difference for management. The urban reservoirs of central India represent the nutrient-linked end of this spectrum. City-adjacent impoundments were found by Unni (1985) to be characterised by low transparency and dominated by cyanobacteria, in contrast to rural waters which were clearer. The characterization of light climate of lakes in the study can be complemented with nephelometric measurement after APHA (2017).

context.prev: 1.11.2 pH The pH level of lake water affects how much hydrogen ion they contain. The buffering system of the ecosystem also depends on this. Most natural freshwaters have a pH between 6 and 9, with the exact value depending on the equilibrium among dissolved CO2, bicarbonate and carbonate ions (Wetzel, 2001). As photosynthesis extracts CO₂ from this equilibrium While respiration returns it the pH in productive shallow lakes generally rises during daytime and falls at night. Dense algal blooms may raise afternoon values above 9, while the buildup of organic matter in stagnant pockets with its attendant CO₂ release drives down the values. The Indian drinking water parameters allow a range of 6.5 to 8.5 (BIS 2012), which is where corrosion, scaling, and physiological stress on aquatic biota become a concern. Seasonally, monsoon inflows dilute alkalinity and may decrease pH, while greater summer concentration and vigorous photosynthesis raise it. Thus, monsoon-type hydrology imposes such dilution- concentration cycles on tropical waters (Talling and Lemoalle 1998). Sewage-fed urban lakes may have a chaotic look. According to Raj and Philip (2025), a study they conducted on Herohalli Lake in North Bangalore, a lake that is being covered in this thesis, revealed that the deposit station was acidic during monsoon and winter (minimum pH 3.59 ± 4.32) against circumneutral summer values of 7.65 ± 1.32, which were due to the decomposition of organic matter that had accumulated at stations receiving treated sewage. The differences in pH level from one station to another make it a good trace of microhabitat conditions throughout a lake.
context.next: 1.11.4 Conductivity Electrical conductivity is the ability of waters to carry an electric current thanks to dissolved ions and is a rapid integrative measure of total mineralisation. The conductivity of freshwaters varies greatly, from a few tens of µS/cm in dilute, rain-fed upland lakes, to several thousand in closed-basin or contaminated waters (Wetzel 2001). In tropical shallow lakes high concentrations of ions can develop because of evaporation and dilution takes place due to rainwater. Conductivity in tropical shallow lakes oscillates with the hydrological year.

input.text: The multi-tube fermentation technique employed in this research evaluates the bacterial density statistically The sample is subjected to serial dilutions that are inoculated into replicate tubes of lactose broth. The pattern of positive and negative tubes, read against probability tables, give the MPN of organisms per 100 ml (APHA 2017). No matter its laborious nature, the method remains the reference procedure for turbid heavily contaminated waters. The standards are demanding. The absence of E is required by both BIS (2012) and WHO (2022). 100 mL of potable water - coli presence. According to CPCB (2008) use-classes, total coliforms are permitted to be 50 MPN/100ml for Class A, 500 for Class B (outdoor bathing) and 5000 for Class C. Urban lakes which receive sewage, treated or otherwise, routinely far exceed even the last figure by orders of magnitude – for example coliform counts as high as 3480000 CFU/100ml have been recorded near the sewage inflows of Hebbal lake (Ravi Kumar and Spoorthi 2025), and a field survey in 2007 found two-thirds of the lakes in Bangalore to be sewage-fed (Ramachandra et al. 2015). In these waters, the MPN index should not be just a number but a public-health message that the fishermen, dhobis, children and cattle using the lake margins, as well as the groundwater of nearby wells. The seasonal change in coliform concentrations, dilution during the monsoon, concentration during dry months, and often a pulse of first-flush contamination, is as much a sanitary question as it is a limnological one. It is an essential part of the physico-chemistry record emanating from this thesis.

context.prev: 1.13 Microbial Parameters: Coliforms and the MPN Index Chemical testing will identify what is in the water but cannot in itself tell us whether the water is safe to touch bathe in or drink. This judgement depends on microbiological evidence, and since pathogenic bacteria and viruses are many, transient and difficult to assay, sanitary science 135 Page 79 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 79 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 60 has long made use of indicator organisms, bacteria that are themselves harmless or nearly so, but whose presence indicates recent faecal contamination and thus the possible presence of pathogens. Among these, Escherichia coli has emerged as the preferred indicator: it is an almost exclusive inhabitant of the gut of warm-blooded animals, it is shed in enormous numbers in faeces, and its detection in water indicates contamination recent enough to carry sanitary risk (Edberg et al. 2000). Total coliforms are a wider group that includes soil and environmental genera and can be viewed as a second index of general bacterial loading and of treatment efficiency.
context.next: 1.14 Eutrophication: Mechanisms, Thresholds and Ecological Succession When we talk about eutrophication, we mean the excess nutrients in a water body and the more production reflecting this phenomenon. Nixon (1995) gave the most widely accepted definition, namely, “an increase in the rate of supply of organic matter to an ecosystem”. This is a deliberate formulation that avoids reference to cause, and it thus applies equally to natural ageing as well as to the accelerated, human-driven process that now dominates. The causes of urban lake pollution in India are straightforward enough. Untreated or partially treated sewage, 162 191 Page 80 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 80 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 detergent-laden grey water, agricultural runoff and horticultural runoff; the result is that lakes built centuries ago as irrigation tanks now function as nutrient sinks in one of the cities’ central parks. Ramachandra et al. 2002; Ramachandra et al. 2024).

input.text: This pattern has been acknowledged by Indian limnology since long. A six-year study of the Bhavanisagar reservoir in the then Madras State by Sreenivasan is a benchmark: the chemistry of the impoundment tracked the monsoon cycle faithfully, with inflow diluting the dissolved load during the wet months and evaporative concentration restoring it as the dry season advanced (Sreenivasan 1964). The community structure of algae in Hyderabad’s fish ponds was affected jointly by temperature and the monsoon rains (Zafar 1967; Munawar 1974). On a comparative survey of 24 reservoirs in central India, urban water bodies were found to be significantly more conductive, less transparent and more frequently dominated by Page 87 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 87 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 68 cyanobacteria than their rural counterparts (Unni 1985). More recent accounts sharpen the same theme. According to Ghosh et al. (2012), in Santragachi lake, West Bengal, monsoon led to a decrease in phytoplankton diversity but improved water quality due to dilution of pollutants due to rains. Summer months experienced peak cyanobacterial occurrence in Bhoj wetland Bhopal with temperature, total dissolved solids and nitrate being the strongest predictors of succession (Ahmed and Wanganeo 2015). According to satellite mapping at the national level, there has been a quantification of the hydrological amplitude of the cycle. Open water occupied 58.5 per cent of the mapped wetland area after the monsoon against 39.4 per cent before the monsoon. This shows a seasonal contraction of around a third (SAC-ISRO 2011).

input.text: Enzymatic inhibition of AChE is a well-established biomarker of exposure to organophosphorous and carbamate insecticides connecting exposure at the synapse to neurotoxic effect at the level of the organism (Fulton and Key 2001). The enzymology of the teleost cholinesterases as well as their use to monitor neurotoxic contamination was set out by Sturm et al. (1999) . The enzyme does not exhibit complete specificity. The presence of metals and detergents can reduce its activity. Moreover, seasonal and temperature variations can affect the baseline (Lionetto et al. 2013). AChE ranks as a biomarkers of effect according to the classification of van der Oost et al. (2003), and where several biomarkers are measured together the integrated biomarker response (IBR) index of Beliaeff and Burgeot (2002) offers a means of combining them into a single comparative score across stations and seasons.

input.text: Figure 11 Schematic framework of the present investigation 122 132 138 185 Page 100 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 100 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 81 1.21 Scope of the Study The study covers one complete hydrological year, from July 2022 to June 2023, resolved into five seasons, and three lakes of Bangalore North chosen to represent a gradient from a large eutrophic water body through a shrunken, highly polluted tank to a shallow, comparatively cleaner one. Within each lake the three-station design separates the open water, the stagnant deposit zone and the wastewater inlet, so that internal heterogeneity can be distinguished from differences among lakes. The physical, chemical and microbial analyses were carried out by standard methods, and the floristic surveys identify algae, hydrophytes and mesophytes to the level of the genus, which is sufficient for the diversity indices and pollution-indicator analyses employed. The eutrophication experiments were conducted in vitro, in small aquaria under controlled temperature and photoperiod, and their purpose is to define threshold nutrient concentrations rather than to reproduce the full complexity of the lake; extrapolation to the field is therefore made with caution. In the same screening spirit, the zebrafish and duckweed assays were used as screening-level assessments of biological effect, not as regulatory determinations of safe concentration, and the exposure durations were those of standard acute and short-term tests. The study does not attempt sediment or fish-tissue residue chemistry, hydrological modelling, or socio-economic survey. Within these limits, the investigation offers a seasonally resolved, comparative and biologically anchored account of three urban wetlands, intended to inform lake management in the city, nutrient targets, station selection for monitoring, and the interpretation of seasonal data, and to serve as a baseline for future, longer- term surveillance.

input.text: The lakes of Bangalore confirm this through empirical work. The Sankey tank and Mallathahalli lake water-quality-index study by Ravikumar et al. (2013) showed that seemingly degraded Mallathahalli water became differentiated from relatively healthy Sankey water precisely because of its higher dissolved solids, conductivity, alkalinity, hardness and chloride – the very parameters one would predict from a sewage-receiving urban lake. In another instance, there have been studies on Lakhota Lake (Gujarat), which was found to be consistently distinguishable from the other four sites based on its ionic and organic parameters over the two-year study (Ruhela et al. 2024). And during the seasonal survey on the Bhuila Lake (Uttar Pradesh), the expected monsoon to summer oscillation of its physico-chemical character was noticed (Jaya et al. 2026). The findings from these studies reveal a pattern: ionic parameters in urban Indian lakes are less dictated by geology and more by the plumbing of the city.

context.prev: Calcium and magnesium contribute hardness and bicarbonates contribute alkalinity. Hence, the two follow a similar seasonal course. Particular mention of alkalinity is required because it 97 147 Page 118 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 118 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 99 buffers ph and supports photosynthetic carbon demand. Most productive Indian lakes have high alkalinity due to catchment weathering and sewage input (Wetzel 2001). Chlorides are conservative in natural waters; however, since domestic sewage has high chlorides, the lakes have diagnostic value through the use of chlorides. High chlorides are one of the classical chemical markers of sewage pollution (APHA 2017). The ionic picture is completed by sulphates and sodium and potassium, the latter two being useful tracers of detergent-bearing wastewater.
context.next: 2.3.4 Nutrients: nitrogen and phosphorus The most ecologically significant of all chemical parameters are the nitrates and phosphates because they gate primary production in freshwaters. The seminal work of Vollenweider (1968) established nitrogen and phosphorus as the engines of cultural eutrophication and suggested the loading framework within which lakes are still assessed, and a long line of work since has refined rather than replaced that conclusion. Studies of many lakes show increasing amounts of algal biomass with total phosphorus and, secondarily, nitrogen (Downing and McCauley 1992). Stream studies show that even benthic algal biomass is determined by nutrient concentrations across hundreds of sites (Dodds et al. 2002). Urban lakes are at one end of limb 2 of the diagram. Norris and Laws (2017) found nutrient concentrations so high in a shallow hypereutrophic urban lake from Hawaii that light, rather than nutrients, has become the limiting factor to further algal growth. Similar results are increasingly reported from the sewage-fed lakes of India as well.

input.text: Individuals have challenged the modern world view. Based on a survey of many lakes, Downing and McCauley (1992) argued for greater attention to nitrogen than the phosphorus- only doctrine allowed, while Guildford and Hecky (2000) found over a wide range of lakes and oceans that signatures of nutrient deficiency did not simply follow total N:total P ratios. Lewis and Wurtsbaugh (2008) presented the most systematic challenge of this contention when they argued that the evidence for phosphorus control had been accepted by scientists with insufficient scepticism. Another notable challenge came from Schindler et al. (2008) himself.

context.heading: 2.1 Introduction
context.prev: 2.6.1 The nutrient paradigm and its critics The seminal work of Vollenweider (1968) for the OECD laid the intellectual foundations of the field. His analysis placed nitrogen and phosphorus at the heart of lake management and advised on loading boundaries between oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic and hypereutrophic states. The experimental evidence emerged from Canada's Experimental Lakes Area, where Schindler (1974) demonstrated that whole lakes dosed with nitrogen and carbon, but not phosphorus, simply would not bloom, and responses to phosphorus additions were 114 176 Page 122 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 122 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 103 immediate. Several years later Schindler (1977) put a community level twist on this: when the supply ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus drops below about 5:1 by atoms, nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria will prevail, since they alone of all the algae can draw nitrogen from air. The phosphorus paradigm created as a result, shaped lake management for a generation (Carpenter et al. 1998).
context.next: This scientist’s thirty-seven-year whole-ecosystem experiment showed that nitrogen fixation compensated for reduced nitrogen inputs so that such reductions alone cannot control eutrophication. The prevailing view is a dual-nutrient view. Phosphorus remains the main lever in most freshwaters but nitrogen control is often necessary too, particularly when the management target is cyanobacterial blooms (Conley et al. 2009; Smith and Schindler 2009).

input.text: 2.6.2 Experimental enrichment and the search for thresholds The question of how much nutrient is too much has been pursued at every scale from the culture flask to the whole lake. At the smallest scale, bioassays of the kind pioneered by Elser et al. (1990), who surveyed phosphorus and nitrogen limitation of phytoplankton growth across North American freshwaters, established that limitation is widespread but not universal, and 100 Page 123 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 123 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 104 that co-limitation by both nutrients is common rather than exceptional. The global meta- analysis of Elser et al. (2007) extended this to terrestrial and marine systems and found that adding nitrogen and phosphorus together produced synergistic responses far more often than either nutrient alone, a result with direct implications for experimental design. Marine and estuarine work points the same way: Smith (2006), comparing ninety-two coastal ecosystems, found phytoplankton biomass responding to enrichment in patterns broadly consistent with the freshwater literature.

context.heading: 2.1 Introduction
context.prev: This discussion is by no means an exercise in academic hairsplitting for the present study: if a standardisation of the minimal concentrations of nitrate and phosphate that trigger an eutrophic response is to be done experimentally, then both nutrients need to be manipulated, singly and together, as the thesis does.
context.next: Mesocosm studies provide the intermediate scale most relevant to this thesis. In Lake Taihu, China, Xu et al. (2010) ran nutrient-addition experiments through the growing season and showed that phytoplankton growth responded to nitrogen and phosphorus inputs in a seasonally shifting pattern, with phosphorus most limiting in winter and nitrogen in summer, evidence that thresholds are not fixed numbers but moving targets set by the season. O'Donnell et al. (2017), working on Lake Baikal, combined spatial surveys with enrichment incubations and demonstrated co-limitation even in that enormous, oligotrophic system. Müller and Mitrovic (2014) reported phytoplankton co-limitation by nitrogen and phosphorus in a shallow eutrophic reservoir, and Stephen et al. (2004), in a small shallow English lake, used mesocosms to separate bottom-up nutrient control from top-down fish control, finding both at work on summer phytoplankton. Havens et al. (1996) ran twenty controlled mesocosm experiments over a year in subtropical Lake Okeechobee and showed that the plankton's response to nutrients depended on when and where in the lake the community was collected. Christensen et al. (1995) predicted, and verified, how the vertical distribution of chlorophyll shifts when the epilimnion of stratified lakes is enriched. Even the attached algal community follows the rule: Mei and Zhang (2015) found periphyton in macrophyte-dominated shallow systems responding clearly to nitrogen and phosphorus enrichment. On the macrophyte side, Smith (2014) showed in field mesocosms that nitrogen and phosphorus together regulate whether floating or submerged plants come to dominate. Perhaps most directly relevant to the in-vitro design of this thesis, Sidelev (2012) demonstrated experimentally that adding nutrients to water from the shallow, highly eutrophic Lake Nero further altered its phytoplankton, showing that even eutrophic water retains enrichment headroom.

input.text: 2.7.2 Hydrophytes: the macrophytes of the water body Aquatic macrophytes, though fewer than three thousand species worldwide, punch far above their numerical weight in lake ecology: they shelter invertebrates and fish fry, stabilise sediments, strip nutrients from the water and, when they run to excess, choke the water body entirely (Chambers et al. 2008). Their distribution within a lake is structured first by the physical environment, light, water depth, water-level fluctuation and exposure, and only secondarily by chemistry (Bornette and Puijalon 2011). The conventional life-form classification into emergent, submerged, floating-leaved and free-floating plants is more than a convenience, because each form interacts with the water column differently and responds differently to enrichment (Chambers et al. 2008). Emergents such as Typha stand astride the 123 199 Page 129 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 129 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 110 water's edge and pump nutrients into rhizomes; submerged plants live or die by underwater light and vanish first when turbidity rises; floating-leaved plants shade the column below; and free-floaters such as Eichhornia and Lemna ride the surface, uncoupled from the sediment and exquisitely sensitive to what the water itself contains (Bornette and Puijalon 2011). This last sensitivity is what qualifies the duckweeds for the bioassay work reviewed later in this chapter, and what makes the composition of a lake's macrophyte cover a readable statement of its Indian macrophyte surveys confirm both the diversity and the stress. Abujam et al. context.prev: Page 128 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 128 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 109 The Indian empirical record is rich and regionally varied. Seasonal phytoplankton surveys have now been published from lakes in every part of the country: Lakshmipuram Lake in Andhra Pradesh, where Pratap et al. (2025) tracked diversity through the year; Komen lake in Meghalaya, where Hajong and Ramanujam (2023) related seasonal diversity shifts to water quality; the subtropical sacred lake of Meghalaya examined by Sharma and Sharma (2022); Mohabala Lake in Maharashtra, where Mahajan (2018) recorded the seasonal turnover of the community; Kharungpat Lake in Manipur, where Salam et al. (2023) tied phytoplankton composition to the physico-chemical environment; a rural Ahmedabad lake in which Mulia et al. (2017) combined diversity counts with Palmer's pollution index; and the saline-alkaline Lonar crater lake, where Kedar and Khobragade (2026) related pre- and post-monsoon phytoplankton to the lake's unusual chemistry. Two generalisations emerge from this body of work. First, chlorophytes and bacillariophytes dominate the cleaner phases and cyanobacteria the enriched ones, regardless of region. Second, the monsoon is the great reset: dilution lowers cell densities and shifts composition, after which the community rebuilds through autumn and winter towards a summer peak. Both generalisations are directly testable in the three Bangalore lakes of the present study, which span a gradient from less polluted to highly eutrophic. The wider wetland community follows the same rules: Packiam et al. (2025), assessing the Vembannur wetland in Tamil Nadu, found macroinvertebrate diversity tracking water quality across the wetland, a reminder that the algal signal at the base of the food web propagates upward to the organisms that graze it. Studies that pair generic identification with diversity indices, as most of the Indian surveys above do, also share a methodological finding: the indices are most informative when read against the water chemistry rather than alone, since a diverse community in enriched water often consists of many tolerant forms rather than many sensitive ones (Washington 1984).

context.prev: 3.6.4.2 Primary Productivity: Light and Dark Bottle Method Primary productivity was measured using the classic technique of oxygen measurement in light and dark bottles. An identical bottle kept dark undergoes only respiration, and so the decline in oxygen measures community respiration. The gross production is obtained by adding the respiration term back. Water samples that had been collected from the three sampling stations were transferred into BOD bottles; one bottle was kept under dark conditions and the Page 189 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 189 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 170 other was kept under light conditions for 24 hours. input.text: Page 222 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 222 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 203 4.2 Standardization of the Minimal Mineral Concentration for Eutrophication and the Study of Ecological Succession (Objective B) The field survey of Section 4.1 established that the three lakes carry a heavy and seasonally variable nutrient load, and that phosphate and nitrate reach their maxima in the winter–spring window that precedes the warm bloom season. That observation raises an obvious experimental question, and it is the question this objective was designed to answer: how much nitrogen and phosphorus does it actually take to tip a body of lake water into a eutrophic bloom, and what sequence of ecological changes accompanies the tipping? To answer it under controlled conditions, a laboratory microcosm experiment was set up in which a mixed algal inoculum drawn from the study lakes was grown in sterile water enriched with a graded series of nitrate and phosphate additions, and followed for fifteen days.

context.heading: 3.10 Summary
context.prev: 4.1.8 Synthesis of Objective A Three conclusions follow from the water-quality data. First, the three lakes are markedly alike in their organic and microbial degradation despite their differing designations: dissolved oxygen, BOD, COD, nitrate, phosphate and coliform counts showed no significant between- Page 221 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 221 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 202 lake difference, all three failed the dissolved-oxygen criterion in roughly three-quarters of samples, and all carried high COD and heavy coliform loads. Second, the one axis on which the lakes differed significantly was dissolved-mineral load (conductivity and TDS), and the post-hoc tests show this to be a single contrast Herohalli distinctly lower than Lingadheeranahalli and Ullal, which did not differ from each other rather than a smooth three- way gradient. Because the least-mineralised lake (Herohalli) was the most organically and microbially degraded, ionic enrichment and organic pollution are separate, here inversely related, dimensions, and no single label or index captures both. Third, the spatial structure within each lake (open water least impaired, inlet most) was stronger and more consistent than the between-lake structure, directing any management response to the inlets. Overlying both was a coherent seasonal cycle: an acidic, turbid, coliform-rich monsoon; an autumn dissolved- oxygen minimum; a winter COD maximum; a winter–spring nutrient maximum that primes the water for blooms; and a warmer, evaporative summer. That nutrient maximum motivates the eutrophication experiment of Section 4.2.
context.next: 4.2.1 Experimental design Seven treatments were established in four-litre microcosms held at 27 ± 2 °C under a 12-hour light : 12-hour dark photoperiod, each inoculated with 100 mL of mixed algal inoculum collected from the lakes. Nitrate (as potassium nitrate) and phosphate (as potassium dihydrogen phosphate) were added in a graded series from a nutrient-free control up to forty times that base level, with the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio held constant at 10 : 1 throughout, following the treatment design in Table 4.5. Chlorophyll-a, algal cell density, dissolved oxygen and water transparency were recorded at five-day intervals (days 0, 5, 10 and 15), and the phytoplankton community was observed for the qualitative changes that define ecological succession. Holding the N : P ratio fixed means that the experiment measures the response to the overall intensity of nutrient enrichment rather than isolating the separate roles of nitrogen and phosphorus; that distinction is returned to in the discussion.

input.text: The consequence for dissolved oxygen was the mirror image of the biomass gain, and it is the heart of the eutrophication story. As algal biomass climbed, dissolved oxygen fell in lock-step: chlorophyll-a and dissolved oxygen were very strongly and negatively correlated across the whole experiment (Pearson r = -0.967, p < 0.001). In the control, oxygen held near saturation (7.4 mg L⁻¹ at day 15); but it declined progressively with dose, and by day 15 it had fallen to 3.5 mg L⁻¹ at T4 and crossed the 3 mg L⁻¹ hypoxia line in T5 and T6 (2.6 and 1.8 mg L⁻¹). This is the paradox of eutrophication made visible in a jar: the same nutrient enrichment that produces a luxuriant surface bloom drives the water below it toward oxygen starvation, because the respiration and microbial decomposition that accompany and follow the bloom consume more oxygen than the system can replace. Water transparency deteriorated in the same ordered way, from fully transparent in the control to a dark-green, scum-covered surface in T6.

input.text: Three results stand out. First, consistent with the water chemistry, the lakes did not differ significantly in productivity: gross productivity averaged 5.73, 5.19 and 7.97 mg L⁻¹ day⁻¹ at Herohalli, Lingadheeranahalli and Ullal (Kruskal–Wallis H = 0.899, p = 0.638, n = 45, ε² = 0.02, small effect), and net productivity and total chlorophyll were likewise non-significant (p = 0.696 and p = 0.299). Second, productivity varied significantly with season (H = 13.128, p = 0.011, n = 45, ε² = 0.298, large effect): gross productivity was highest in the monsoon (10.6 mg L⁻¹ day⁻¹) and lowest in summer (3.2), and the Dunn–Holm post-hoc test attributes the seasonal effect specifically to the monsoon–summer contrast (adjusted p = 0.003), the only pairwise comparison to reach significance. Third, productivity increased from the open water (4.76 mg L⁻¹ day⁻¹) to the nutrient-rich inlet (7.54 mg L⁻¹ day⁻¹), the highest single values being at the Ullal inlet in the monsoon (gross 22.3, net 20.9 mg L⁻¹ day⁻¹). These values agree closely with the author's companion measurements on the same lakes (Raj and Philip, 2025).

context.next: 4.3.4 Synthesis of Objective C The productivity and biodiversity evidence gives a consistent ecological reading of the three lakes. All three are highly and comparably productive, with no significant between-lake difference in gross or net productivity or chlorophyll; productivity is raised in the monsoon by nutrient inflow and at the nutrient-rich inlet stations, and the standing algal crop peaks in summer. Their communities are those of enriched, disturbed water: pollution-tolerant green algae and cyanobacteria, a sparse macrophyte flora of eutrophication indicators, and a riparian fringe in which invasive species are prominent, most of all at Ullal. The lakes differ in the composition rather than the quantity of their biodiversity: marginal-plant richness is lowest at the shrunken Lingadheeranahalli, and the three floras overlap little. This is the biological Page 235 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 235 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 216 counterpart of the physico-chemical result: three lakes similar in the severity of their enrichment, distinct in its local expression.

input.text: The between-lake difference in heart rate was significant (Kruskal–Wallis H = 10.609, p = 0.005, n = 27, ε² = 0.408, large effect). context.prev: 4.5.1 Zebrafish embryo: heart rate and somite development Embryos were exposed to water from each station of each lake and their heart rate counted at the torpedo stage in three independent experiments (normal range ≈ 120–180 BPM). Water from Herohalli and Ullal produced only mild cardiac depression (lake-mean heart rates 110.7 and 108.0 BPM; the Ullal open water was highest at 124.7 BPM), with stations otherwise between about 90 and 125 BPM. Lingadheeranahalli was more toxic: its open and deposit waters were the most bradycardic of the non-lethal exposures (means near 99.3 and 93.0 BPM), and its inlet water was lethal in two of the three experiments the embryos had no detectable heartbeat (0 BPM), the third registering 64, for a station mean of 21.3 BPM. This is embryonic mortality and is the most acute toxic response recorded in the study.

input.text: All analyses were performed in Python 3 using the SciPy and scikit-posthocs libraries.

context.heading: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
context.prev: The statistical treatment was as follows. The distribution of each variable was first tested for normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test; normality was rejected (p < 0.05) for 16 of 16 parameters, most at p < 0.001, so non-parametric methods were adopted throughout. Differences among the three lakes, and among the five seasons, were tested with the Kruskal-Wallis H test (α = 0.05). For every test the exact H statistic, the p-value, the sample size n and an effect size are reported; the effect size is epsilon-squared (ε² = H(n+1)/(n²−1)), interpreted by the conventional bands of ≈ 0.01 small, ≈ 0.06 medium and ≈ 0.14 large. Where an omnibus Kruskal-Wallis test was significant, pairwise differences were localised with Dunn's post-hoc test using the Holm correction for multiple comparisons, and the adjusted pairwise p-values are given. Monotonic associations between variables were quantified with Spearman's rank-correlation coefficient.
context.next: Page 282 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 282 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 263 5.1 Objective A: Comparative Assessment of Water Quality The first objective was a comparative assessment of the water quality of the three lakes on physico-chemical, microbial and biological grounds. Nineteen physico-chemical variables and the most-probable-number (MPN) index of coliforms were measured each month at each of the three stations, giving a matrix of some two thousand five hundred observations over the year. The purpose of this section is not to recite that matrix but to draw out of it the structure that matters: how the three lakes differ from one another, how the three stations differ within each lake, and how the whole assemblage moves with the seasons. The account begins with the physical regime, proceeds through the oxygen economy, the dissolved mineral load and the nutrient status, turns then to the microbial evidence, and closes by drawing the parameters together through their correlation structure and a composite Water Quality Index.

input.text: The three lakes did not differ significantly in pH over the year (Kruskal-Wallis H = 0.256, p = 0.880, n = 108, ε² = 0.002, negligible effect), and the acidity was general across the open, deposit and inlet stations rather than localised. The isolated December pH of 0.53 in the Herohalli deposit water is not credible for a standing lake (it corresponds to a strong mineral acid), is treated as an instrument or recording artefact, and accounts for the inflated winter standard deviation (± 1.67) in the Herohalli profile.

context.next: This acidic signature departs from much of the earlier Bengaluru work, which more often reports neutral to alkaline lake water; Arafath et al. (2008) recorded pH 7.9-9.2 at Ullal itself, and the CES-IISc surveys generally describe circum-neutral to alkaline conditions (Ramachandra et al., 2015). It is, however, consistent with the author's companion measurements on these same lakes, in which Herohalli open water ranged from about 5.35 in autumn to 7.50 in summer (Raj and Philip, 2025). The agreement of two independent datasets on the same water bodies, and the orderly rise from an acidic monsoon minimum to a near- neutral summer, indicate that the low pH is a real feature of the sampling period rather than a systematic error, most plausibly reflecting the organic-acid load delivered by decomposing matter and untreated inflow during the wet season and its progressive neutralisation as the water warmed toward summer. The divergence from the older, more alkaline records is nonetheless noted rather than resolved.

input.text: Electrical conductivity, a proxy for dissolved ionic load, produced the clearest between-lake signal of any physical variable and differed significantly among the lakes (Kruskal-Wallis H = 28.862, p < 0.001, n = 108, ε² = 0.27, a large effect). The post-hoc test localises this difference precisely: Herohalli differed significantly from both Lingadheeranahalli and Ullal (Dunn-Holm p < 0.001 in each case), whereas Lingadheeranahalli and Ullal did not differ from one another (p = 0.88). The pattern is therefore not a smooth three-way gradient but a single contrast: Herohalli (median 313 µS cm⁻¹) was distinctly the least mineralised, while Lingadheeranahalli and Ullal (medians 519 and 588 µS cm⁻¹) carried a similar, higher ionic load. Notably, Herohalli the least mineralised lake proved to be the most organically and microbially degraded (Sections 4.1.3, 4.1.6), so ionic enrichment and organic pollution are distinct and, here, inversely related axes.

context.heading: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
context.prev: Turbidity exceeded the BIS acceptable limit of 5 NTU in the great majority of samples (86% at Herohalli, 58% at Lingadheeranahalli and 56% at Ullal). Herohalli was the most turbid lake, with a monsoon mean of 52.0 ± 15.0 NTU as the first rains transported suspended solids into the lake, declining through autumn and spring. Lingadheeranahalli and Ullal were clearer in the main water body but showed episodic pulses, notably a high-variance winter spike at Lingadheeranahalli (29.2 ± 44.1 NTU) driven by a single turbid month at one station. The inlet stations were the most turbid in every lake, consistent with their role as entry points for run- off. The monsoon-led pattern at Herohalli and the episodic pulses elsewhere are consistent with the rainfall-driven suspended-solid loading reported for other Indian urban lakes. Persistently high turbidity limits light penetration, with consequences for productivity examined in Section 4.3.
context.next: Page 297 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 Page 297 of 401 - Integrity Submission Submission ID trn:oid:::3117:616484955 278 Superimposed on this baseline were episodic excursions. Herohalli's winter conductivity mean of 1505.8 ± 1982.3 µS cm⁻¹ reflects a single extreme deposit-water reading (7380 µS cm⁻¹ in December) rather than a lake-wide shift; away from that pulse the lake sat near 285-300 µS cm⁻¹. Ullal's spring mean of 3901 ± 245 µS cm⁻¹, confined to its deposit and inlet stations, indicates a concentrated point-source ionic input during the dry pre-monsoon period. These spikes remain below the chronic 1200-2800 µS cm⁻¹ conductivities reported for Bellandur (Ramachandra et al., 2017) and, except at their peaks, within the CPCB Class E irrigation criterion of 2250 µS cm⁻¹. The conductivity and total-dissolved-solids structure is shown in Figures 4.5 and 4.6.

COD was high in every lake and season an order of magnitude or more above the ~10 mg L⁻¹ typical of clean surface water and peaked in winter (266.7 ± 97.8 mg L⁻¹ at Herohalli, 282.7 ± 113.5 mg L⁻¹ at Lingadheeranahalli, 245.3 ± 60.6 mg L⁻¹ at Ullal), when decomposable organic matter accumulated under cool, low-flushing conditions. input.text: Expressed as a specific growth rate over the fifteen days, the enrichment gradient translated into a smooth, saturating rise in algal growth: from 0.014 day⁻¹ in the control through 0.265 day⁻¹ at T3 and 0.295 day⁻¹ at T4 to 0.338 day⁻¹ at T6. The growth rate climbed most steeply between the control and T3-T4 and then began to level off, the classic signature of a system passing from nutrient limitation into nutrient saturation. Algal cell density traced chlorophyll almost exactly the two were essentially collinear across all treatments and days (Pearson r = 0.997, p < 0.001) which is an important internal validation that the chlorophyll signal reflects real phytoplankton proliferation rather than pigment artefact. The growth curves are shown, on both linear and logarithmic axes, in the microcosm chlorophyll results, and the density and oxygen trajectories in the microcosm oxygen and cell-density results.

Chlorophyll-a, the direct measure of algal biomass, barely moved in the nutrient-free control (from 0.22 to 0.27 mg L⁻¹ over the fortnight, a 1.2-fold change) but rose steeply and in strict proportion to the dose in every enriched microcosm, reaching 20.85 mg L⁻¹ in T4 and 39.5 mg L⁻¹ in T6 by day 15 an eighty- three-fold and a one-hundred-and-fifty-eight-fold increase respectively (Table 5.12).
context.next: The consequence for dissolved oxygen was the mirror image of the biomass gain, and it is the heart of the eutrophication story. As algal biomass climbed, dissolved oxygen fell in lock-step: chlorophyll-a and dissolved oxygen were very strongly and negatively correlated across the whole experiment (Pearson r = -0.967, p < 0.001). In the control, oxygen held near saturation (7.4 mg L⁻¹ at day 15); but it declined progressively with dose, and by day 15 it had fallen to 3.5 mg L⁻¹ at T4 and crossed the 3 mg L⁻¹ hypoxia line in T5 and T6 (2.6 and 1.8 mg L⁻¹). This is the paradox of eutrophication made visible in a jar: the same nutrient enrichment that produces a luxuriant surface bloom drives the water below it toward oxygen starvation, because the respiration and microbial decomposition that accompany and follow the bloom consume more oxygen than the system can replace. Water transparency deteriorated in the same ordered way, from fully transparent in the control to a dark-green, scum-covered surface in T6.

input.text: 3.1 Overview of the Research Design This study looked at the limnological parameters, toxicants and their impact on the fishes and macro invertebrates of the three lakes. Apart from documenting the limnology and toxicology of the lakes, this study is also detailed in attempting to predict the ecological fate of the three wetlands. Each lake was sampled at three hydrologically and ecologically distinct stations – Open Surface Water, Deposit Water and Inlet Water every month for twelve consecutive months, from July 2022 to June 2023, so that the full annual cycle of seasons was captured.
